items.stem: Explain the difference between parody and adaptation.
items.answer: Parody imitates in order to mock or criticise; adaptation transforms a text into a new form or context, often seeking to preserve its meaning for a new audience.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why intertextuality is useful for writers of non-literary texts such as adverts.
items.answer: Borrowing familiar stories, phrases or images gives an advert instant meaning, emotional associations and humour with very few words. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Leila writes: "Intertextuality only means quoting other books." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It includes allusion, parody, pastiche, adaptation, genre conventions and any way a text's meaning depends on other texts, including visual and non-literary ones.
items.markingKey: It includes allusion, parody, pastiche, adaptation, genre conventions and any way a text's meaning depends on other texts, including visual and non-literary ones. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a disability-rights activist at a rally outside a parliament.

They say we ask for special treatment. Ramps are not special. Captions are not special. A lift that works is not special. What is special is a parliament with three hundred steps and not one ramp to its public gallery. We have watched our laws being made from the pavement for long enough. Nothing about us, without us.

Identify the intertextual reference in this text and explain how it shapes meaning.
items.answer: The closing slogan "Nothing about us without us" is borrowed from the disability-rights movement, connecting the speech to a collective history of activism.
items.markingKey: The closing slogan "Nothing about us without us" is borrowed from the disability-rights movement, connecting the speech to a collective history of activism. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following editorial cartoon, described in words.

[A technology billionaire stands on a vast stage wearing nothing but a branded lanyard, arms raised in triumph. A giant screen behind him reads 'REVOLUTIONARY'. Rows of investors in suits applaud wildly. In the front row a small child holds up a hand-written sign: 'IT'S JUST A PHONE.']

Identify the intertextual reference in this text and explain how it shapes meaning.
items.answer: The cartoon depends on intertextual knowledge of Andersen's "The Emperor's New Clothes": readers recognise the child's honesty and the crowd's pretence, so the cartoon's meaning comes from mapping the old story onto the new situation.
items.markingKey: The cartoon depends on intertextual knowledge of Andersen's "The Emperor's New Clothes": readers recognise the child's honesty and the crowd's pretence, so the cartoon's meaning comes from mapping the old story onto the new situation. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "All texts are intertextual."

items.stem:
Read the following fan fiction based on Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice' (an original extract written for study).

Charlotte Lucas did not love Mr Collins. She had never expected to. What she loved, she discovered in the first week at Hunsford, was the small sitting room at the back of the parsonage, where he never came because the light was poor. There she read, and wrote letters to Elizabeth, and was, for two hours each afternoon, nobody's wife.

Analyse how the writer uses an earlier text or genre to create meaning.
items.answer: It depends on the reader knowing Pride and Prejudice: Charlotte marries Mr Collins for security, and Austen's narrator views her mainly through Elizabeth's disappointment; the fan fiction answers back to that perspective.

items.stem:
Read the following parody advertisement created by a student activist group (culture jamming).

[Image: a glossy fashion-advert layout. A model in a neon crop top poses, smiling, in front of a landfill heaped with clothes.]
WEAR IT ONCE. POST IT. BIN IT.
New season, new you – every week.
*Made by someone paid less in a month than this top costs in a day.
#OutfitOfTheMinute

Identify the genre or text type of this extract and explain how it follows or subverts its conventions.

In this text, for example: "#OutfitOfTheMinute" (parody hashtag) and the glossy layout combined with a landfill background, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.

items.stem:
Read the following satirical news story from a parody website.

Local man Darren Cole, 41, has once again shown extraordinary courage by sharing a news article on social media without reading beyond the headline. 'I didn't need to,' Cole explained. 'The headline already agreed with me.' Friends describe the gesture as 'very on brand'. At press time, Cole was furiously defending the article's second paragraph, which he believes says something it does not.

Analyse how this text borrows the conventions of another genre and to what effect.
items.answer: Target: confirmation bias and careless sharing. Methods: mock-heroic diction, an "everyman" figure, ironic self-incrimination in quotation, parody of news clichés; the reader is invited to recognise themselves.
items.markingKey: Target: confirmation bias and careless sharing. items.stem:
Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']
[Panel 3: the leader, sweating, looks away: 'Next question.']

Which conventions does this text use, and how does it use them to create meaning?
items.answer: It is a cartoon. Conventions: a single image or panels, caricature, captions or speech bubbles and visual exaggeration for comment. In this text, for example: "a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw" (anthropomorphism) and the three-panel set-up, question and punchline, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.
items.markingKey: It is a cartoon. Conventions: a single image or panels, caricature, captions or speech bubbles and visual exaggeration for comment. items.stem:
Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Explain what global issue this text shares with a literary work you have studied.
items.answer: Power, propaganda and the representation of gender in wartime. Supporting feature: "THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT. YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE." (parallelism) – the matching structure makes factory work equal to fighting and binds the reader to the soldiers.
items.markingKey: Power, propaganda and the representation of gender in wartime. Supporting feature: "THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT. YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE." (parallelism) – the matching structure makes factory work equal to fighting and binds the reader to the soldiers. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

My father's boat goes out like a held breath;
the harbour waits, the water keeps its counsel.

Now the boat is a planter on the quay,
full of geraniums. The water still keeps its counsel,
but no one asks it anything.

items.stem:
Read the following satirical column from a news-parody website.

In a bold move hailed by absolutely everyone in the Cabinet, the government announced today that the housing crisis will henceforth be known as the 'housing opportunity'. 'Language matters,' said the Minister, speaking from the second of his four homes. 'Young people aren't priced out – they're simply enjoying an extended stay with their parents, which is wonderful for family values.' A spokesperson confirmed that rents would remain the same, but would now feel more optimistic.

Evaluate how the text uses genre conventions to criticise its target.
items.answer: Target: governments that replace policy with spin. Methods: a deadpan news register, mock euphemism ("housing opportunity"), ironic detail (four homes), and bathos ("feel more optimistic"); incongruity between serious form and absurd content creates the humour.

items.stem: Distinguish between parody and adaptation.
items.answer: Parody imitates in order to mock or criticise; adaptation transforms a text into a new form or context, often seeking to preserve its meaning for a new audience.
items.markingKey: Parody imitates in order to mock or criticise; adaptation transforms a text into a new form or context, often seeking to preserve its meaning for a new audience. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following satirical news story from a parody website.

Local man Darren Cole, 41, has once again shown extraordinary courage by sharing a news article on social media without reading beyond the headline. 'I didn't need to,' Cole explained. 'The headline already agreed with me.' Friends describe the gesture as 'very on brand'. At press time, Cole was furiously defending the article's second paragraph, which he believes says something it does not.

Evaluate how the text uses genre conventions to criticise its target.
items.answer: Target: confirmation bias and careless sharing. Methods: mock-heroic diction, an "everyman" figure, ironic self-incrimination in quotation, parody of news clichés; the reader is invited to recognise themselves.
items.markingKey: Target: confirmation bias and careless sharing. Methods: mock-heroic diction, an "everyman" figure, ironic self-incrimination in quotation, parody of news clichés; the reader is invited to recognise themselves. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column published in a national newspaper.

Let me be clear: I am no technophobe. I file this column from a laptop, on a train, while my phone buzzes like a trapped wasp. But I have watched my own students in Nairobi sit side by side at lunch, heads bowed, in total silence, as if at a funeral. We would never let a casino open in a school corridor. Why, then, do we allow a slot machine in every pocket?

Discuss how the concept of communication could link this text to a work of a different genre.
items.answer: Communication: the column argues that phones replace face-to-face communication with silence.
items.markingKey: Communication: the column argues that phones replace face-to-face communication with silence. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following fan fiction based on Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice' (an original extract written for study).

Charlotte Lucas did not love Mr Collins. She had never expected to. What she loved, she discovered in the first week at Hunsford, was the small sitting room at the back of the parsonage, where he never came because the light was poor. There she read, and wrote letters to Elizabeth, and was, for two hours each afternoon, nobody's wife.

Identify the intertextual reference in this text and explain how it shapes meaning.
items.answer: It depends on the reader knowing Pride and Prejudice: Charlotte marries Mr Collins for security, and Austen's narrator views her mainly through Elizabeth's disappointment; the fan fiction answers back to that perspective.
items.markingKey: It depends on the reader knowing Pride and Prejudice: Charlotte marries Mr Collins for security, and Austen's narrator views her mainly through Elizabeth's disappointment; the fan fiction answers back to that perspective. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following single-panel editorial cartoon, described in words.

[A giant smartphone towers over a family dinner table like a skyscraper. The parents and two children sit at its base, each gazing up at its glowing screen. Their plates are untouched. Under the table, the family dog looks up at the reader. Speech bubble from the dog: 'Remember when they used to drop food?']

Identify the genre or text type of this extract and explain how it follows or subverts its conventions.
items.answer: It is a cartoon. Conventions: a single image or panels, caricature, captions or speech bubbles and visual exaggeration for comment. In this text, for example: "'Remember when they used to drop food?'" (ironic speech bubble) and the placement of the dog looking out at the reader, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience.
items.markingKey: It is a cartoon. Conventions: a single image or panels, caricature, captions or speech bubbles and visual exaggeration for comment. In this text, for example: "'Remember when they used to drop food?'" (ironic speech bubble) and the placement of the dog looking out at the reader, each used to serve the text's purpose for its audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following two short poems from the same (fictional) poetry collection.

Poem 1: 'Tide'
My father's boat goes out like a held breath;
the harbour waits, the water keeps its counsel.

Poem 2: 'Tide (II)'
Now the boat is a planter on the quay,
full of geraniums. The water still keeps its counsel,
but no one asks it anything.

How could this text be compared with a literary work you have studied through the concept of transformation?
items.answer: Transformation: the community and its objects are transformed by economic change.
items.markingKey: Transformation: the community and its objects are transformed by economic change. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "All texts are intertextual."
items.answer: In a broad sense all texts are intertextual, but analysis should focus on deliberate, meaningful connections.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every text uses inherited language, genres and conventions; readers interpret through other texts they know. Arguments against: some texts make intertextuality central and others do not; the term loses precision if applied to everything. Supported judgement: In a broad sense all texts are intertextual, but analysis should focus on deliberate, meaningful connections.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Genre is more important to the reader than to the writer."
items.answer: Genre is a shared contract: writers use it to shape meaning and readers to interpret it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: readers use genre to interpret and choose texts; expectations shape reading. Arguments against: writers choose genres to reach audiences; subversion requires the writer's awareness. Supported judgement: Genre is a shared contract: writers use it to shape meaning and readers to interpret it. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following review of a film adaptation of a classic novel, from an arts website.

Three stars. The new adaptation of Jane Eyre is beautiful to look at and curiously cold to feel. Every candle-lit corridor is gorgeously framed; every gust of moorland wind arrives on cue. What is missing is Jane's voice – the furious, funny first person that makes the novel a confession rather than a costume drama. Without it, she becomes someone things happen to, rather than someone who tells us what they meant.

Discuss how the concept of transformation could link this text to a work of a different genre.
items.answer: Transformation: adaptation transforms narrative voice into images.
items.markingKey: Transformation: adaptation transforms narrative voice into images. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.
